sentence: We will show that no matter which k numbers are removed from {1, 2, …, 100}: • When k = 9 it is NOT always possible to choose 9 numbers from the survivors which add up to 100.
sentence-category-reason: States the conclusion for k=9 (not always possible), presenting an explicit answer.

sentence: • When k = 8 it is always possible to choose 8 numbers from the survivors that add up to 100.
sentence-category-reason: States the conclusion for k=8 (always possible), presenting an explicit answer.

sentence: In what follows we explain one way of arriving at these answers.
sentence-category-reason: Outlines the plan to explain how the answers are obtained.
Introduces the next case to be considered, indicating the next step.

sentence: Suppose 9 numbers are removed (that is, deleted from {1,…, 100}) so that 91 numbers remain.
sentence-category-reason: Sets up the scenario for k=9 by restating the given condition.

sentence: The question is: must there always be some 9‐element subset of the survivors whose sum is exactly 100?
sentence-category-reason: Restates the specific question to be answered for k=9.

sentence:
A counter‐example shows that the answer is “no.” For instance, remove the 9 smallest numbers from {1,…,100}, namely remove
  1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9.
sentence-category-reason: Constructs a counterexample by specifying which numbers to remove.

sentence: Then the survivors are {10, 11, 12, …, 100}.
sentence-category-reason: States the resulting survivor set after the specified deletion.

sentence: Now notice that any 9 distinct numbers chosen from these survivors are at least 10 each.
sentence-category-reason: Infers a property of any 9 chosen numbers from the survivors (each at least 10).

sentence:
Hence, if you choose any 9 numbers you get a sum at least
  10 + 11 + … + 18.
sentence-category-reason: Deduces a lower bound for the sum of any 9 chosen numbers from the survivors.

sentence:
A quick computation shows that:
  10 + 11 + … + 18 = 9×(10+18)/2 = 9×14 = 126.
sentence-category-reason: Performs the explicit computation of the lower-bound sum.

sentence: That sum is well above 100.
sentence-category-reason: Concludes by comparing the computed bound to 100 to support impossibility.

sentence: (In fact, since every element is “shifted up”, every 9‐element subset of {10, …, 100} will have an even larger sum.
sentence-category-reason: Provides further reasoning that all such sums are even larger due to shifting.

sentence: ) Thus in this deletion scenario no 9‐subset can have sum 100.
sentence-category-reason: Draws the conclusion for this deletion scenario (no 9-subset sums to 100).

sentence: In other words, with k = 9 a “bad” deletion is possible.
sentence-category-reason: Restates the overall result for k=9 (a bad deletion exists), i.e., the answer to part (a).
Introduces the next case to analyze (k=8), indicating the next step.

sentence: Now suppose 8 numbers are removed, leaving 92 survivors.
sentence-category-reason: Sets up the scenario for k=8 by restating the given condition.

sentence: We wish to know if, regardless of which 8 numbers are deleted from {1,…,100}, one can always find eight distinct survivors whose sum is exactly 100.
sentence-category-reason: Restates the specific question to be answered for k=8.

sentence:
A particularly instructive “worst‐case” deletion is to remove the 8 smallest numbers:
  1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8.
sentence-category-reason: Constructs a particular deletion (worst-case) by specifying numbers removed.

sentence: Then the survivors are {9, 10, …, 100}.
sentence-category-reason: States the resulting survivor set after the specified deletion.

sentence: In this case, what is the smallest possible sum for an 8–subset?
sentence-category-reason: Sets the next step by asking to determine the minimum possible sum of an 8-element subset.

sentence: It is achieved by taking the eight smallest survivors {9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16}.
sentence-category-reason: States the conceptual claim that the minimum is achieved by the eight smallest survivors, without calculation.
Writes the explicit sum expression to compute the total.

sentence:
A short calculation groups these numbers in pairs:
  (9+16) + (10+15) + (11+14) + (12+13) = 25 + 25 + 25 + 25 = 100.
sentence-category-reason: Performs the computation by pairing terms to sum to 100.

sentence: Thus, even in this extremal case the eight survivors {9, 10, …, 16} add up to 100.
sentence-category-reason: Concludes from the computation that this extremal subset sums to 100.

sentence: It turns out that one can show (by a “smoothing” or “exchange‐argument” method that uses the fact that the eight survivors come from all of {1,…,100} except 8, and hence, by “adjusting” any nearly minimal 8–subset one can achieve the total 100) that no matter which 8 numbers are removed, there is always some 8–subset among the survivors with sum 100.
sentence-category-reason: Explains, at a high level, a general argument (smoothing/exchange) guaranteeing existence of a sum-100 subset.

sentence: (The idea is that after 8 numbers are removed, the minimum sum achievable by an 8–subset is never forced above 100 — and when it is exactly 100, there is nothing more to do.
sentence-category-reason: Further conceptual explanation of why the minimum achievable sum does not exceed 100.

sentence: Thus for k = 8 the answer is “yes.
sentence-category-reason: States the conclusion for k = 8.

sentence: (a) k = 9: There is a deletion (for example, deleting 1,2,…,9) after which every 9–subset has sum at least 126.
sentence-category-reason: Summarizes the reasoning for k = 9 with an example deletion and its implication.

sentence: So it is not always possible to find 9 survivors summing to 100.
sentence-category-reason: Concludes the answer for part (a).

sentence: (b) k = 8: No matter how one deletes 8 numbers, one can always choose eight survivors (in the worst case, the eight smallest survivors) that add to exactly 100.
sentence-category-reason: States the conclusion for part (b) including the worst-case subset.

sentence:
So the final answers are:
 (a) No.
 (b) Yes.
